title: The Grammar of a Sentence
bigQuestion: What makes a group of words into a sentence that works?

story.title: The Sentence That Would Not Stop
story.kicker: Devon reads his own paragraph aloud, and about halfway through he runs out of air.
paragraphs: Mr. Alvarez asks Devon to read his paragraph to the class. Devon stands up. He takes a breath and starts. "On Saturday we went to the beach and it was hot and my cousin brought a kite and the wind was strong and the kite went up and then the string broke and we ran after it and a dog got there first." Devon's face turns red. He has not stopped once. He has not taken a breath.

The class laughs, but not in a mean way. A girl named Priya says, "That is one sentence? I got lost after the kite." Devon looks at his paper. She is right. It is one sentence. It is a sentence with eight little sentences stuffed inside it, all tied together with the word and.

Mr. Alvarez writes the whole thing on the board. Then he hands Devon a marker. "Find the places where you could stop," he says. Devon reads it again, slowly. He puts a period after hot. He puts one after kite. He puts one after broke. Now the paragraph has four sentences. He reads it again. This time he breathes.

"Nothing changed in the story," Mr. Alvarez says. "The beach is still hot. The dog still wins. But now a reader can follow you." He taps the board. "That is what grammar is for. Not to trap you. To help people follow you."

Devon sits down. He is still a little red. But he writes something at the top of his paper: Stop and breathe. This chapter is about the parts of a sentence and how they fit, so that every reader can follow you all the way to the dog.
story.think: Devon's story did not change when he added periods. So what did change, and why did it matter to the class?

lessons.title: Subject and Predicate
lessons.mainIdea: Every sentence has a subject (who or what) and a predicate (what happens), and it needs both.
reading: Look at this sentence: The dog got there first. Ask, who is this about? The dog. That part is the *subject*. Now ask, what did the dog do? Got there first. That part is the *predicate*. Every full sentence has both parts. Take one away and it falls apart.

The subject is the who or the what. It can be one word or several: Devon. My cousin's red kite. The strong wind at the beach. The predicate is the rest. It holds the action or tells what the subject is. Devon laughed. My cousin's red kite went up. The wind at the beach was strong.

Here is a quick test. Cover the subject with your hand. Does the rest still tell what happened? Cover the predicate. Does the rest still tell who? If either half is missing, you do not have a sentence yet. You have a piece of one.

words.d: the part of a sentence that tells who or what the sentence is about
the part of a sentence that tells what the subject does or is

look.title: Two Halves on the Board
look.text: Mr. Alvarez draws a line down the middle of the board. On the left he writes: The little brown dog. My cousin. The kite string. On the right he writes: broke with a snap. ran across the sand. barked at the waves. He asks the class to match a left side to a right side to make a sentence that makes sense.
look.prompt: Which left side goes with which right side? Could any left side match more than one right side?

check.q: In the sentence 'The wind was strong,' what is the subject?
check.why: The subject tells who or what the sentence is about. It is about the wind.

check.q: What does the predicate of a sentence do?
choices: Tells what the subject does or is
Ends the sentence with a mark
Names who the sentence is about
check.why: The predicate holds the action or tells what the subject is. 'Got there first' is a predicate.

check.q: 'My cousin's red kite' has no predicate. What is it?
check.why: It names a what, but nothing happens. Without a predicate, it is only a piece of a sentence.

lessons.title: Nouns and Pronouns
lessons.mainIdea: Nouns name people, places, things and ideas, and pronouns stand in for nouns so you do not repeat them.
reading: Read this: Priya lost Priya's pencil, so Priya asked Devon if Devon had seen Priya's pencil. Ouch. Now read this: Priya lost her pencil, so she asked Devon if he had seen it. Much better. The words her, she, he and it took the place of the names. Those words are *pronouns*.

First, the names. A *noun* is a word that names a person, a place, a thing or an idea. Priya, beach, kite and courage are all nouns. Some nouns name one thing: dog. Some name more than one: dogs. A noun that names one special person or place gets a capital letter: Devon, Chicago, Lake Michigan.

A pronoun stands in for a noun. I, you, he, she, it, we and they are the common ones. Here is the rule that matters: the reader must know which noun the pronoun replaces. Priya asked Devon, and he said no. Who said no? Devon, because he is the closest boy. If two boys were there, you would need the name again.

words.d: a word that names a person, a place, a thing or an idea
a word like she, it or they that stands in for a noun

look.title: Nouns in a Short Story
look.prompt: Which kind of noun shows up most in this story? Why might a story about a beach day be full of thing-nouns?

check.q: Which word is a noun?
check.why: A noun names a thing. 'Kite' names a thing. The others are a verb, an adverb and a pronoun.

check.q: Why do writers use pronouns?
choices: To repeat a name so no one forgets it
To stand in for a noun so it is not repeated
To show who is the most important
check.why: Pronouns like she and it take the place of nouns. That keeps the sentence from repeating a name over and over.

check.q: Which noun should have a capital letter?
check.why: Chicago names one special place. Nouns that name a special person or place get a capital.

lessons.title: Verbs, Adjectives and Adverbs
lessons.mainIdea: Verbs show action or being, adjectives describe nouns, and adverbs describe verbs.
reading: The kite went up. The kite is the noun. Went is the *verb*, the word that shows the action. Some verbs show a strong action: ran, snapped, barked. Some verbs show being, not doing: is, was, are. The sand was hot. Nothing moves, but was is still the verb.

Now add some color. The red kite went up. Red tells you more about the kite. A word that describes a noun is an *adjective*. The strong wind. A tiny dog. Three cousins. Adjectives answer which one, what kind, or how many.

One more. The kite went up fast. Fast tells you how it went up. A word that describes a verb is an *adverb*. Adverbs answer how, when or where. Many end in -ly: slowly, loudly, suddenly. The dog barked loudly. Loudly describes barked. Here is a trick: an adjective sticks to a noun, and an adverb sticks to a verb.

words.d: a word that shows an action (ran) or a state of being (is, was)
a word that describes a noun: red, tiny, three
a word that describes a verb and tells how, when or where: slowly, later, here

look.title: One Sentence, Built Up
look.text: The dog ran. The brown dog ran. The brown dog ran quickly. The small brown dog ran quickly across the wet sand and barked happily at the waves.
look.prompt: Which words are adjectives here? Which are adverbs? What does each one add that the first sentence did not have?

check.q: In 'The sand was hot,' which word is the verb?
check.why: 'Was' is a being verb. It does not show action, but it is still the verb.

check.q: What does an adjective describe?
check.why: Adjectives like red and tiny describe nouns. They tell which one, what kind or how many.

check.q: In 'The dog barked loudly,' what does 'loudly' tell you?
check.why: 'Loudly' is an adverb. It describes the verb barked and tells how.

lessons.title: Prepositions Show Where and When
lessons.mainIdea: A preposition is a small word like under, on or after that links a noun to the rest of the sentence.
reading: Where is the dog? The dog is under the table. On the table. Beside the table. Behind the table. Each little word tells you where the dog is. Those little words are *prepositions*. They link a noun (the table) to the rest of the sentence.

Prepositions can tell where: in, on, under, over, beside, between, across. They can tell when: before, after, during, until. They can tell other things too: with, for, about, of. A preposition never stands alone. It always comes with a noun or pronoun after it: after lunch, with my cousin, about the kite.

The preposition plus its noun is called a *phrase*. A phrase is a group of words that works together but is not a whole sentence. The string broke over the water. Over the water tells where. Take the phrase away and you still have a sentence: The string broke. Add it back and the reader can see the place.

words.d: a small word like under, on, after or with that links a noun to the rest of the sentence
a group of words that works together but is not a whole sentence

look.title: Move the Dog
look.text: Picture a small dog and a big red chair. Now say where the dog is, using one new little word each time. The dog is on the chair. The dog is under the chair. The dog is behind the chair. The dog is beside the chair. The dog jumps over the chair. Each time, the dog moves, and only one word changed.
look.prompt: Which word changed each time? What would happen to the picture if you took that word out and just said 'The dog is the chair'?

check.q: Which word is a preposition?
check.why: 'Under' links a noun to the rest of the sentence and tells where. It is a preposition.

check.q: What always comes after a preposition?
check.why: A preposition never stands alone. It needs a noun or pronoun: under the table, with him.

check.q: In 'We ate lunch after the race,' what does 'after the race' tell you?
check.why: 'After' is a preposition that tells when. The phrase 'after the race' tells the time of lunch.

lessons.title: Simple and Compound
lessons.mainIdea: A simple sentence has one subject and one predicate; a compound sentence joins two with a comma and a joining word.
reading: The wind blew. That is a *simple sentence*. One subject, one predicate, one complete thought. The kite went up. That is another. Two short sentences in a row can sound choppy. So writers join them: The wind blew, and the kite went up. Now it is one *compound sentence*.

Look at what holds the two halves together: a comma and the word and. The words and, but, or and so are joining words, also called *conjunctions*. Each one means something different. And adds. But shows a change. Or gives a choice. So shows a result. The string broke, so the kite flew away.

Here is the rule for the comma. When you join two full sentences with a conjunction, put a comma before the conjunction. The dog got there first, but Devon did not care. Both halves could stand alone, so the comma goes in. If the second half cannot stand alone, no comma: Devon laughed and sat down.

words.d: a sentence with one subject and one predicate that gives one complete thought
two simple sentences joined with a comma and a conjunction like and, but, or so
a joining word such as and, but, or, so

look.title: Same Story, Two Ways
rows: Version B: some joined into compounds
Version C: everything joined with and
look.prompt: Version C is Devon's one-breath paragraph. Version A is choppy. Why might Version B be the easiest to read?

check.q: Which one is a compound sentence?
choices: The wind blew, and the kite went up.
check.why: Two full sentences joined by a comma and 'and' make a compound sentence.

check.q: Which conjunction shows a result?
check.why: 'So' shows that one thing caused another: The string broke, so the kite flew away.

check.q: Where does the comma go in a compound sentence?
check.why: The comma goes right before the joining word: 'The dog got there first, but Devon did not care.'

lessons.title: Complex Sentences
lessons.mainIdea: A complex sentence joins a full sentence to a part that cannot stand alone, using words like because, when or although.
reading: Read this: When the string broke. Something is missing. You want to ask, what happened then? Now read: When the string broke, the kite flew away. There it is. The first part cannot stand alone. It leans on the second part. Together they make a *complex sentence*.

The part that cannot stand alone is a *dependent clause*. It depends on the rest. It starts with a word like because, when, if, although, after, before or since. The part that can stand alone is the main part: the kite flew away. A complex sentence has one of each.

The order can go either way. When the string broke, the kite flew away. Or: The kite flew away when the string broke. Notice the comma. If the dependent part comes first, put a comma after it. If it comes second, you usually need no comma. Complex sentences let you show why, when and what if.

words.d: a sentence with one main part and one dependent part that cannot stand alone
a part of a sentence that starts with a word like because or when and cannot stand alone

look.title: A Famous Sentence From Illinois
look.text: Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.
look.cite: Abraham Lincoln of Illinois, the Gettysburg Address, 1863
look.prompt: This is one long sentence. Find the subject and the main verb. Then find at least one phrase that tells when or where.

check.q: Which is a dependent clause?
check.why: 'Because the wind was strong' starts with because and cannot stand alone. It needs a main part.

check.q: When does a complex sentence need a comma?
choices: When the dependent part comes first
check.why: 'When the string broke, the kite flew away' needs the comma. 'The kite flew away when the string broke' does not.

check.q: What can a complex sentence show that a simple one cannot?
check.why: Words like because and when connect two ideas and show why, when or what if.

lessons.title: Fragments Are Missing a Part
lessons.mainIdea: A fragment is a piece of a sentence that is missing a subject or a predicate, and you fix it by adding the missing part.
reading: Read this: Ran after the kite. Who ran? You cannot tell. Now this: The kite over the water. What did the kite do? Nothing happens. Each of these is a *fragment*. A fragment looks like a sentence. It starts with a capital and ends with a period. But a part is missing.

There are two ways a fragment usually breaks. Either the subject is gone: Ran after the kite. Or the predicate is gone: The kite over the water. Sometimes a dependent clause is left alone: Because the dog was faster. That is a fragment too. It still needs a main part.

The fix is simple. Ask what is missing and add it. Ran after the kite becomes We ran after the kite. The kite over the water becomes The kite hung over the water. Because the dog was faster becomes Because the dog was faster, it won. Read your sentence aloud. If it leaves you waiting, it is a fragment.

words.d: a piece of a sentence that is missing a subject, a predicate or a main part

look.title: The Note on the Fridge
look.text: A note on the fridge says: Went to the store. Back at five. Milk in the bag. Nobody in the house is confused. They know Mom wrote it, and they know what she means. But every line is a fragment. Now imagine the same lines in a school report about a trip to a store.
look.prompt: Why are fragments fine on a fridge note but not in a report? What would you add to each line to make it a full sentence?

check.q: Which one is a fragment?
check.why: 'Ran after the kite' has no subject. Nobody is named as running. It is a fragment.

check.q: How do you fix a fragment?
check.why: A fragment is missing a subject, a predicate or a main part. Add the missing part and it becomes a sentence.

check.q: 'Because the dog was faster.' What is wrong?
choices: It is a dependent part with no main part
check.why: The clause starts with because and cannot stand alone. It needs a main part such as 'it won.'

lessons.title: Run-ons Never Stop
lessons.mainIdea: A run-on jams two or more sentences together without the right stop, and you fix it with a period, a comma and a conjunction, or a joining word like because.
reading: Devon's beach paragraph was a *run-on*. It had nine sentences tied together with and. A run-on is two or more full sentences that run into each other without the right stop. Here is a short one: The string broke the kite flew away. Two full sentences, no stop at all.

Some run-ons have a comma where a period should be. It was hot, we swam. That is called a comma splice, and it is still a run-on. A comma alone is too weak to hold two full sentences apart. It needs help.

You have three good fixes. One: use a period. The string broke. The kite flew away. Two: use a comma plus a conjunction. The string broke, so the kite flew away. Three: use a word like because or when. When the string broke, the kite flew away. Pick the fix that fits what you mean. Any of them lets the reader breathe.

words.d: two or more full sentences jammed together without the right stop between them
a run-on where only a comma sits between two full sentences

look.title: Words Between the Breaths
look.prompt: A reader usually breathes at a period. How many words did Devon's class have to hold in their heads at once before the fix? After?

check.q: Which one is a run-on?
choices: The string broke, so the kite flew away.
When the string broke, the kite flew away.
The string broke the kite flew away.
check.why: Two full sentences with nothing between them is a run-on. The others each have a proper stop or joining.

check.q: What is a comma splice?
choices: Two full sentences with only a comma between them
A missing comma in a list
check.why: A comma alone cannot hold two full sentences apart. 'It was hot, we swam' is a comma splice.

check.q: Which is NOT a good fix for a run-on?
choices: Use a comma and a conjunction
check.why: Stringing more sentences together with and makes the run-on worse. Devon's paragraph proved it.

lessons.title: Subject and Verb Agree
lessons.mainIdea: A singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject takes a plural verb, and they must match.
reading: The dog barks. The dogs bark. Say them out loud. When the subject is one dog, the verb is barks. When there are two or more dogs, the verb is bark. The subject and the verb *agree*. They match in number. One dog, barks. Many dogs, bark.

It feels backward, and that trips people up. Adding -s to a noun makes it plural: dogs. Adding -s to a verb makes it singular: barks. So a plural subject usually takes a verb with no -s. The kids run. The kid runs. The waves crash. The wave crashes.

The tricky ones are is and are, was and were, has and have. She is here. They are here. He was late. We were late. It has a tail. They have tails. Watch out for words in between: The box of kites is heavy. The subject is box, not kites. Box is one thing, so the verb is is.

words.d: to match in number: a singular subject with a singular verb, a plural subject with a plural verb
one of something
more than one of something

look.title: Spot the Mismatch
look.text: My cousins likes the beach. The wind push the kite up high. A bag of shells sit by the towel. The dog and the boy runs to the water.
look.prompt: Each sentence has a subject and verb that do not agree. Find the subject in each, decide if it is one or more than one, and fix the verb.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
check.why: Dogs is plural, so the verb is bark with no -s.

check.q: In 'The box of kites is heavy,' why is the verb 'is' and not 'are'?
choices: The subject is box, which is one thing
check.why: The subject is box. 'Of kites' is only a phrase in between. One box is heavy.

check.q: Which pair matches?
check.why: He is singular, and was is the singular past form. The others mix singular and plural.

lessons.title: Past, Present, Future
lessons.mainIdea: A verb's tense tells when something happens, and a piece of writing should stay in one tense unless the time really changes.
reading: The kite flies. The kite flew. The kite will fly. Same kite, same action, three different times. The form of the verb tells you when. That is called *tense*. Present tense is now: flies. Past tense is before now: flew. Future tense is later: will fly.

Most verbs make the past by adding -ed: jump, jumped. walk, walked. But many common verbs change in other ways. These are *irregular verbs*, and you learn them by ear and by heart. Go, went. Run, ran. See, saw. Eat, ate. Break, broke. Nobody says goed or breaked.

Here is the rule that matters most in writing. Pick a tense and stay in it. Read this: We went to the beach and my cousin brings a kite. Went is past, brings is present. The reader stumbles. Fix it: We went to the beach and my cousin brought a kite. Change tense only when the time really changes.

words.d: the form of a verb that tells when something happens: past, present or future
a verb that does not make its past tense with -ed, like go and went

look.title: Regular or Not?
rows: Verbs that add -ed (laughed, snapped, barked, wanted)
Verbs that change another way (went, ran, broke, got, was)
Verbs that stay the same (put, hit)
look.prompt: Nearly half of these verbs do not add -ed. Why does a writer need to know the irregular ones by heart?

check.q: Which verb is in the future tense?
check.why: 'Will' plus a verb shows a time that has not come yet.

check.q: What is the past tense of 'break'?
check.why: Break is irregular. Its past tense is broke, not breaked.

check.q: 'We went to the beach and my cousin brings a kite.' What is wrong?
choices: The tense changes for no reason
check.why: Went is past and brings is present. The time did not change, so the verb should be brought.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Word
lessons.mainIdea: Words that sound the same are spelled differently for a reason, and the words you choose should fit where you are and who is listening.
reading: Read this: There going to they're house over their. Every word is said right, and every one is spelled wrong. Their, there and they're sound the same. They are *homophones*. Their shows owning: their house. There points to a place: over there. They're is short for they are: they're going. Fixed: They're going to their house over there.

Other pairs trip people up too. Your and you're. Its and it's. To, too and two. The test is the same each time. Say the long form. If it's can become it is, use the apostrophe. If not, use its. The dog wagged its tail. It's a good dog.

Word choice also depends on where you are. With friends you might say, Yo, that kite was sick. In a class talk or a letter to the principal, you use *formal English*: That kite flew very well. Formal English uses full sentences, no slang, and no text-speak. Neither way is bad. A good writer knows which one fits the room.

words.d: words that sound the same but are spelled differently and mean different things
careful, full-sentence English for school, work and people you do not know well

look.title: Two Messages, One Kite
look.text: Devon sends his friend a text: kite broke lol dog got it first. Then he writes a note to the lifeguard who helped him find it: Thank you for helping me find my kite. The dog reached it before I did, but you got it back. Both messages tell the truth. Both say the same thing. They do not sound the same.
look.prompt: Why did Devon write the two messages so differently? What would happen if he swapped them?

check.q: Which sentence uses the right word?
check.why: 'They're' is short for 'they are.' They are going to the beach.

check.q: 'The dog wagged ___ tail.' Which fits?
check.why: The tail belongs to the dog. 'Its' shows owning. 'It's' would mean 'it is.'

check.q: When should you use formal English?
choices: In every text to a friend
In a class talk or a letter to the principal
check.why: Formal English fits school, work and people you do not know well. With friends, casual talk is fine.

review.q: What two parts does every full sentence need?
review.why: The subject tells who or what. The predicate tells what happens. A sentence needs both.

review.q: In 'The tiny dog barked loudly,' which word is an adverb?
review.why: 'Loudly' describes the verb barked and tells how. That makes it an adverb.

review.q: Which word is a preposition in 'The kite hung over the water'?
review.why: 'Over' links the noun water to the rest of the sentence and tells where.

choices: It was hot so we swam.
It was hot, so we swam.
It was hot so, we swam.
review.why: Two full sentences joined by a conjunction take a comma before the conjunction.

review.q: 'After the rain stopped.' What kind of problem is this?
review.why: It is a dependent clause with no main part. It leaves the reader waiting, so it is a fragment.

review.q: Which is the best fix for 'The bell rang the kids ran out'?
choices: The bell rang and the kids ran out and it was loud
The bell rang, the kids ran out.
When the bell rang, the kids ran out.
The bell rang the kids, ran out.
review.why: A word like when joins the two ideas properly. A comma alone makes a comma splice, and more ands make a longer run-on.

review.q: Which sentence has a subject and verb that agree?
choices: The kids runs to the water.
The kids run to the water.
The kid run to the water.
The kids is running to the water.
review.why: Kids is plural, so the verb is run with no -s.
'Their' shows owning. The kite belongs to them. The other sentences need there or they're.
